title: Right speech
hookLine: no lying, no divisive speech, no harsh speech, no idle chatter (MN 117)

cards: I'm five minutes away, typed by someone who hasn't left the house yet. A story about a coworker, told while she's out at lunch. A reply with a little edge on it.

A long voice memo that could have been one sentence. None of these is a crime. Set side by side, though, they make a fairly complete map of how talk goes wrong, and the Buddha drew that same map in four lines.
Right intention was the direction set inside. Now the first factor of the path that comes out of the mouth: right speech.

teach.b: Sammā vācā. Sammā: right, whole, complete. Vācā: speech, the voice.
In the great forty sutta, the Buddha defines it with four abstentions: from false speech; from divisive speech, the kind that splits people apart; from harsh speech; and from idle chatter.
Four guards at the door of the mouth. Two things stand out. First, the five precepts lay Buddhists take name only one of these, not lying.
Right speech asks for all four. Second, the last guard.
Idle chatter, samphappalāpa in Pali, is talk that goes nowhere: words to fill a silence, gossip with no purpose, saying things only to be heard. And it sits on the same list as lying.
That doesn't make small talk forbidden; many kind words are small. Some teachers put the test as purpose: is this going anywhere good? The same sutta also sets right speech inside a circle.
Right view recognizes wrong speech as wrong. Right effort works to let it go. Right mindfulness stays present while you do.
So speech isn't mended by a rule alone; three other factors run around it.
Why would a path to freedom spend a whole factor on talk? Because speech is where intention first touches another person. You set the direction inside; now it comes out loud.
And talk runs all day long, so the chances to practice do too.

how: Lay Buddhists take the fourth precept, not to speak falsely, often reciting it in Pali at the temple; right speech as a path factor adds abstaining from divisive, harsh and idle speech, and monastics keep detailed rules about speech in their discipline.

o: speaking only in formal, polite language
saying exactly what you think, always
speech free of lies, splitting, harshness, chatter

games.q: what's inside right speech: tap the pairs.

s: idle chatter is on the same list as lying
MN 117 names four kinds of speech to give up, and idle chatter is the fourth.
right speech forbids all small talk
some teachers put the test as purpose: is this going anywhere good? many kind words are small.
the five precepts already cover all four parts of right speech
the precept names only false speech; right speech asks for all four.

games.q: a friend asks you to tell their boss they're sick. they're at the beach. which of the four guards is on duty?
games.why: it's the first guard: abstaining from false speech, first of the four in MN 117, and the one the fourth precept names.

practice: Let your mind replay the last day's talk, like scrolling back through your messages, and sort it without judging: anything not quite true, anything said about someone who wasn't there, anything sharp, anything said only to fill the quiet?
Notice which guard was the sleepiest. Then let the replay go, and rest a while in the silence, where no words are needed.

wordCard.voice: Sammā vācā. Right speech: no lying, no divisive words, no harsh words, no idle chatter. The third factor of the path.

orig.note: Pali sammā vācā: right, or whole, speech, the third factor of the eightfold path.

carryVoice: Your line: four guards. True, uniting, gentle, worth saying. A full year of days, and still going.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 117 (Mahacattarisaka Sutta, the great forty)
